```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
```

This vignette goes from the coding sequences (CDS) of two species to a table of dN, dS and dN/dS for their
ortholog pairs, and to what should be checked before the numbers are read. Everything runs inside R: no program
is started, nothing is downloaded, no file is written. It takes a few seconds.

```{r}
library(coalr)
```

## The data

The package ships a small synthetic example (the files of `examples/dnds` in COAL's repository): two "species"
with 13 coding sequences each, of which 12 are orthologs of each other, and the table that says which gene goes
with which. In real work the two FASTA files are the CDS files of two genomes, **one sequence per gene** (see
"One record is one gene" below), and the pairs come from an ortholog search.

```{r}
dir <- system.file("extdata", package = "coalr")
a <- coal_read_fasta(file.path(dir, "species_a_cds.fasta"))
b <- coal_read_fasta(file.path(dir, "species_b_cds.fasta"))
length(a); length(b)
substr(a[1:2], 1, 60)
pairs <- read.delim(file.path(dir, "orthologs.tsv"))[, 1:2]
head(pairs, 3)
```

`coal_read_fasta()` returns a named character vector. The functions also take a `DNAStringSet`, the list
`seqinr::read.fasta()` returns, a two-column data frame, or the file name itself.

## dN/dS for the pairs

For every pair, `coal_dnds_pairs()` translates both sequences, aligns the two proteins globally
(Needleman-Wunsch, BLOSUM62), threads the codons onto that alignment and estimates dN and dS. The default method
is `"YN"` (Yang and Nielsen 2000).

```{r}
res <- coal_dnds_pairs(a, b, pairs = pairs)
res[, c("seq1", "seq2", "method", "dN", "dS", "dNdS", "codons_compared", "prot_identity", "status")]
```

One row per pair and method. `dN` and `dS` are substitutions per nonsynonymous and per synonymous site, `dNdS`
their ratio; `SE_dN` and `SE_dS` are standard errors of dN and of dS (there is none for the ratio).
`codons_compared` is the number of codon columns the estimate rests on, `prot_identity` the identity of the
protein alignment in percent. A pair that cannot be computed does not stop the call: its row has
`status = "error"` and the reason in `note`.

Several methods at once (the rows of a pair then follow each other). `method =` is accepted for `methods =`:

```{r}
both <- coal_dnds_pairs(a, b, pairs = pairs[1:3, ], methods = c("YN", "NG"))
both[, c("seq1", "method", "dN", "dS", "dNdS")]
```

The example was simulated with a known dN/dS per gene (`simulated_omega` in `orthologs.tsv`), so the estimates
can be compared with the truth:

```{r}
truth <- read.delim(file.path(dir, "orthologs.tsv"))
data.frame(gene = res$seq1, simulated = truth$simulated_omega, estimated = round(res$dNdS, 3))
```

With 200 to 400 codons per gene the estimates scatter around the simulated values; that scatter is what a
single pair can tell you.

## Before reading the numbers

Status `ok` means that the method produced numbers, not that they are informative. Three things are worth a
flag: few compared codons, a saturated synonymous distance, and a pair of proteins that are hardly alike.
`min_codons`, `max_ds` and `min_identity` mark such rows. They never drop a row and never change a number: the
status becomes `warning` and `note` says why.

```{r}
flagged <- coal_dnds_pairs(a, b, pairs = pairs, min_codons = 250, max_ds = 0.6, min_identity = 80)
flagged[, c("seq1", "dS", "codons_compared", "prot_identity", "status", "note")]
attr(flagged, "flagged")
```

(The thresholds here are chosen so that this small example shows each flag; common starting points for real
data are `min_codons = 50`, `max_ds = 2` and `min_identity = 30`.) Filter afterwards, in the open:

```{r}
keep <- subset(flagged, status == "ok")
nrow(keep)
summary(keep$dNdS)
```

`dNdS` is `NA` when dS is below 1e-6 (two sequences without a synonymous difference have no ratio), and very
small dS values give unstable ratios for no biological reason: look at `dS` before interpreting a large `dNdS`.

## The alignments behind the numbers

`keep_alignments = TRUE` returns the protein and codon alignment of every pair, for a look at a pair that
surprises you:

```{r}
one <- coal_dnds_pairs(a, b, pairs = pairs[2, ], keep_alignments = TRUE)
aln <- attr(one, "alignments")
substr(c(aln$protein1, aln$protein2), 1, 70)
substr(c(aln$codon1, aln$codon2), 1, 70)
```

## One record is one gene

Every sequence is treated as a gene. CDS files from genome annotations (Ensembl, NCBI, TAIR) usually hold every
transcript of every gene; with such a file one gene gives several rows with different values, and an ortholog
search splits its best hits between the transcripts. Give one sequence per gene. A simple and common choice is
the longest CDS of each gene; here for IDs of the form `gene.1`, `gene.2`:

```{r}
tx <- c(G1.1 = "ATGGCTAAAGGTCTGGAACGTTAA", G1.2 = "ATGGCTAAAGGTCTGGAACGTGGTCTGTAA", G2.1 = "ATGAAACCCGGGTTTTAG")
gene <- sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", names(tx))
longest <- tx[unlist(lapply(split(seq_along(tx), gene), function(i) i[which.max(nchar(tx[i]))]))]
names(longest)
```

`coal pipeline --longest-isoform` (below) does this for the usual header styles and says what it did.

## Genes of another genetic code

`code` is the NCBI genetic code, one per call (default 1, the standard code). Mitochondrial genes need their
own call with their own code, for example `code = 2` for vertebrate mitochondria; translated with the standard
code they have internal stop codons (`coal_translate(x, details = TRUE)$internal_stops`) and their estimates
mean nothing. The methods `"Comeron"` and `"Li"` are implemented for the standard code only.

## When COAL should also find the orthologs

`coal_dnds_pairs()` needs the pairs. The complete pipeline (translation, DIAMOND reciprocal best hits, alignment,
dN/dS, a run report) is the `coal pipeline` command, which `coal_pipeline_pairs()` runs through Python; it needs
the Python package `coal-align` and DIAMOND, so it is not run here:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
out <- coal_pipeline_pairs(file.path(dir, "species_a_cds.fasta"), file.path(dir, "species_b_cds.fasta"),
                           threads = 4, longest_isoform = TRUE, min_codons = 50, max_ds = 2)
head(out$pairs)        # the same columns as above
out$report$cite        # what to cite for this run
```

For gene families there is `coal_dnds_clusters()` (every pair within each cluster, with a per-cluster summary).
`?coalr` has a table of the command line's options and the R arguments that correspond to them.

## What to cite

COAL's numbers come from published methods, in code derived from KaKs_Calculator 2.0 and PAML. For a result
obtained as above cite COAL (with its version, `coal_info()$coal_version`), PAL2NAL for the codon alignment
method (Suyama, Torrents and Bork 2006), the estimator (for `"YN"`: Yang and Nielsen 2000) and the program the
code is derived from (Wang et al. 2010, KaKs_Calculator 2.0; Yang 2007, PAML 4). The command `coal cite` lists
the references for every method, with their DOIs.

```{r}
coal_info()$coal_version
```
